OXID Payment Base

A platform-agnostic, payment-provider-agnostic foundation for OXID 7.5+.

Events. Smart-Contracts. SOLID. Abstract. One core that every PSP, every shipping carrier, every returns workflow plugs into — without ever importing each other.

Package
oxid-esales/payment-base
Architecture
Event-Driven · PSR-14
Built on
OXID eShop 7.5+ · PHP 8.2+
Reference impls
Stripe · PayPal · OpalReturns
What Payment Base provides
Four pillars · one PSP-agnostic core
The provider-agnostic core

Payment Base provides
four pillars.

Payment Base (oxid-esales/payment-base) is the layer below every PSP module (Stripe, PayPal, …), every returns flow (OpalReturns), and every shipping integration. PSPs and downstream modules never import each other — they share only Payment Base.

1

Admin “Payment” tab

One shared tab on the OXID admin Order Details page. PSPs contribute panels via a tagged service oe.payment.admin_panel — no per-PSP admin tabs.

2

Domain models

PaymentContract aggregate, BasketSnapshot value object, Transaction, ContractCondition, ContractState enum. Owns all 6 database tables.

3

Event system

PSR-14 EventDispatcher, request-scoped EventContext, HandlerInterface, 30+ events. Anyone can introduce a new event.

4

Smart-Contracts

State machine DRAFT → … → FULFILLED with extensible conditions (payment_authorized, fraud_check, …). Early-Order-Creation pattern out of the box.

Six abstract base classes. ContractCreationHandler, AbstractPaymentCaptureService, AbstractPaymentRefundService, AbstractWebhookProcessor, AbstractHandler, AbstractFileLoggerFactory — you extend, you don’t copy.
~25 interfaces. PaymentAdapterInterface, ShopAdapterInterface, SessionAdapterInterface, repository & service interfaces. The boundary rule — if it’s provider-agnostic, it lives here.
Architecture invariants. PSPs are peers. opalreturns is PSP-agnostic. No direct contract mutations in controllers. Grep guards in pre-commit enforce the lines.

Pillar 3 · Event system
EventDispatcher · EventContext · HandlerInterface

Anyone can introduce a new event.
Handlers are tagged services. No central switch statements.

The three primitives
interface EventDispatcherInterface {
    public function dispatch(EventInterface $event): EventInterface;
    public function addListener(
        string $eventClass,
        callable $listener,
        int $priority = 0
    ): void;
}

interface EventContextInterface {
    public function get(string $key, mixed $default = null): mixed;
    public function set(string $key, mixed $value): void;
    public function getContract(): ?PaymentContractInterface;
    public function getBasket(): ?object;
    public function getUser(): ?object;
}

interface HandlerInterface {
    public function handle(object $event): void;
    public static function getHandledEventClass(): string;
    // Optional: public function getPriority(): int;
}
Registration — one line of YAML
Your\Module\Handler\YourHandler:
    tags:
        - { name: payment.event_handler, priority: 50 }

(StripeCheckoutSessionRequest,

PayPalCaptureRequest, …)"] CC["ContractCreatedEvent"] CDC["ContractDraftCompletedEvent"] CTP["ContractTransitionedToPendingEvent"] CCF["ContractConditionFulfilledEvent"] CRC["ContractReadyToCommitEvent"] CCM["ContractCommittedEvent"] CFU["ContractFulfilledEvent"] CTE["ContractCancelled / Expired / FailedEvent"] PI["PaymentInitiatedEvent"] PA["PaymentAuthorizedEvent"] PCAP["PaymentCapturedEvent"] PR["PaymentRefundedEvent"] PF["PaymentFailedEvent"] OC["OrderCreatedEvent / OrderCompletedEvent"] WR["WebhookReceivedEvent"] EI --> CEI EI --> PEI EI --> PSP CEI --> CC & CDC & CTP & CCF & CRC & CCM & CFU & CTE PEI --> PI & PA & PCAP & PR & PF & OC & WR style EI fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#1e40af,stroke-width:2px,color:#0b1424 style CEI fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#b45309,color:#0b1424 style PEI fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#b45309,color:#0b1424 style PSP fill:#e9d5ff,stroke:#7e22ce,color:#0b1424
Priority rules: 100+ contract creation (core) · 80–99 order creation (core) · 50–79 your validation/enrichment · 1–49 your post-processing · 0 default. Context is request-scoped: handler with priority 100 sets it, handler with priority 0 reads it. Never modify the event — pass via context.

Pillar 4 · Smart-Contracts
State machine + extensible conditions + early order creation

A Smart-Contract is the source of truth.
The order is a downstream effect.

When the customer clicks “Place Order”, Payment Base does not create an order — it creates a PaymentContract. The contract carries an immutable BasketSnapshot and a list of conditions that must be fulfilled before commitment. The order is created early (in NOT_FINISHED state) so its order number is available before redirecting to the PSP.

Contract lifecycle · with hook points
flowchart TB D[DRAFT] --> NF[NOT_FINISHED] NF --> P[PENDING] P --> A[AUTHORIZED] A --> R[READY_TO_COMMIT] R --> CO[COMMITTED] CO --> F[FULFILLED] A -. condition: payment_authorized .-> R A -. condition: fraud_check .-> R A -. condition: stock_reserved .-> R F2[CANCELLED / EXPIRED / FAILED
terminal alternatives] style D fill:#fff,stroke:#8390ad style NF fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#1e40af,color:#0b1424 style P fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#b45309,color:#0b1424 style A fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#b45309,color:#0b1424 style R fill:#e9d5ff,stroke:#7e22ce,color:#0b1424 style CO fill:#d1fae5,stroke:#047857,color:#0b1424 style F fill:#d1fae5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:3px,color:#0b1424 style F2 fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#0b1424
Why early order creation
  • Order number available before the PSP session is created
  • PSP dashboard (Stripe / PayPal) shows the order number in metadata — reconciliation works on day 1
  • Order exists before payment completion — no race with webhooks
  • Order finalisation (COMMITTED) only when all conditions are met
Conditions are extensible
$contract->addCondition(
    new ContractCondition(
        type: 'subscription_verified',
        data: ['plan_id' => 'pro_monthly']
    )
);

// Later, in your event handler:
$contract->fulfilCondition(
    'subscription_verified',
    ['verified_at' => '2026-05-08T10:23:00Z']
);

// When ALL conditions are fulfilled:
//   ContractReadyToCommitEvent dispatched
//   StripeOrderCreationHandler / your handler finalises
The hook points are the state transitions. Each Contract…Event is a place your extension can intercept. Your code never mutates a contract directly — you dispatch an event, a handler mutates. Grep guards in one-page-checkout/bin/pre-commit-check.sh enforce this.

Build a PSP module · 1 of 3
The boundary rule · six extension mechanisms

Six extension mechanisms.
Zero modifications to Payment Base core.

The boundary rule

If it could work with another PSP — it lives in payment-base.

If it touches \Stripe\StripeClient or PayPal SDK concepts — it lives in the PSP module.

PayPal and Stripe are peers. They share only Payment Base. Architecture grep guards in each PSP’s pre-commit-check.sh block any cross-import.

File layout convention
extensions/your-psp/
├── src/
│   ├── Adapter/        # YourPspAdapter
│   ├── EventSystem/
│   │   ├── Event/      # YourPsp...RequestEvent
│   │   └── Handler/    # YourPsp...Handler
│   ├── Service/        # YourPsp business services
│   └── Webhook/        # YourPspWebhookProcessor
├── services.yaml       # the wiring
└── tests/Unit + Integration
Six mechanisms · pick the smallest one that fits
1
Event Handler
Subscribe to a contract / payment event. The default extension point.
Low
2
Service Override via DI
Replace or decorate a service binding in services.yaml. Inheritance + Symfony aliasing.
Medium
3
Contract Metadata
Store custom data on a contract via setMetadata(). Survives the lifecycle.
Low
4
Webhook Handler Addition
Handle a new PSP webhook event type. Extends AbstractWebhookProcessor.
Medium
5
Controller Extension
Add UI or logic to existing checkout / admin pages. Use only for thin orchestration.
Medium
6
Adapter Decoration
Wrap StripeAdapter / PayPalAdapter for marketplace headers, logging, retries.
High

Build a PSP module · 2 of 3
Adapter + ContractCreationHandler template

Implement PaymentAdapterInterface.
Extend ContractCreationHandler. That’s the spine.

1. Adapter — bridge the PSP SDK
class StripeAdapter implements PaymentAdapterInterface
{
    public function createPayment(
        CreatePaymentRequest $req
    ): PaymentResponse {
        $pi = $this->stripe->paymentIntents->create([
            'amount'   => $this->toCents($req->getAmount()),
            'currency' => strtolower($req->getCurrency()),
            'metadata' => $req->getMetadata(),
        ]);
        return new PaymentResponse(
            providerPaymentId: $pi->id,
            status: $this->mapStatus($pi->status),
            amount: $req->getAmount(),
            currency: $req->getCurrency(),
            requiresAction: $pi->status === 'requires_action',
            clientSecret: $pi->client_secret,
        );
    }
    // capture / refund / authorize / void / 3DS / vault …
}
2. Template-method handler
class StripeContractCreationHandler
    extends ContractCreationHandler
{
    protected function afterContractCreated(
        PaymentContractInterface $c,
        EventContextInterface $ctx
    ): void {
        $c->setMetadata('payment_method', $this->methodFrom($ctx));
        $ctx->set('contractId', $c->getId());
    }
    // Base class handles repo save + event dispatch.
}

services.yaml · tagged iterator
StripeContractCreationHandler:
    tags:
      - { name: payment.event_handler, priority: 100 }

EventListenerProviderInterface:
    class: EventListenerProvider
    arguments:
      - !tagged_iterator payment.event_handler
Adding a whole new PSP requires zero modifications to payment-base. A new adapter, a new factory, a new ContractCreationHandler subclass, register in services.yaml. The core stays untouched — that’s the SOLID Open/Closed promise.

Webhook processor + admin Payment tab contribution

Webhooks & admin operations finish the spine.
Both ride the same event bus.

Webhook processor · extends abstract base
class StripeWebhookProcessor
    extends AbstractWebhookProcessor
{
    protected function verifySignature(
        string $payload, array $headers
    ): bool {
        return $this->adapter->verifyWebhookSignature(
            $payload, $headers['Stripe-Signature'], $this->secret
        );
    }

    protected function routeEvent(WebhookEvent $e): void {
        match ($e->getType()) {
            'payment_intent.succeeded' =>
                $this->dispatcher->dispatch(
                    new PaymentAuthorizedEvent($contract, $ctx)),
            'charge.refunded' =>
                $this->dispatcher->dispatch(
                    new PaymentRefundedEvent($contract, $ctx)),
            // …
        };
    }
}

// Idempotency & logging come from the abstract base.
// Provider-agnostic WebhookLogRepository persists every call.
Capture / Refund services
class StripeCaptureService
    extends AbstractPaymentCaptureService
{
    protected function executeCapture(
        PaymentContractInterface $c, ?float $amount
    ): CaptureResponse {
        return $this->adapter->captureAuthorization(
            new CaptureAuthorizationRequest(
                authorizationId: $c->getProviderOrderId(),
                amount: $amount ? (string) $amount : null,
            )
        );
    }
}
// Partial capture: $amount <= PaymentIntent.amount, irreversible
// Partial refund: total_refunded + amount <= captured
Payment tab · PSP-agnostic, panel-providers contribute

One tab. Every PSP.

Payment Base owns the “Payment” tab on the OXID admin Order Details page (since Sprint I). PSPs do not ship per-PSP admin-order tabs.

Each PSP contributes one or more panel-provider services, tagged oe.payment.admin_panel. Payment Base’s tab collects them via !tagged_iterator.

# stripe/services.yaml
StripeOrderRefundPanelProvider:
    tags:
      - { name: oe.payment.admin_panel,
          provider: stripe, priority: 100 }

# Order Refund flow uses shared admin services
OrderRefundViewDataProvider:    # cached PI/charge fetch
    arguments: ['@stripe.adapter']
OrderActionDispatcher:          # dispatches capture/refund events
    arguments: ['@event.dispatcher']
Admin operations ride the same events
  • Admin clicks “Capture” → OrderActionDispatcher dispatches StripeCaptureRequestEvent
  • StripeCaptureRequestHandler (priority 0) executes via the adapter
  • oe_payments_transaction records the audit trail; OXPAID updated by OrderPaymentCompletedHandler
  • Self-healing on view: reconcilePaymentState() repairs OXPAID if Stripe Dashboard bypassed the webhook chain
The whole spine is reusable. A second PSP — PayPal — ships exactly the same shape: adapter + 4 events + 6 handlers + webhook processor + 1 panel provider. Stripe and PayPal are peers: neither imports the other; both share Payment Base.

Consumer 1 · OpalReturns
A PSP-agnostic returns module on Payment Base

OpalReturns is the proof:
a real consumer, zero PSP imports.

OpalReturns handles refund & return workflows across every PSP — Stripe, PayPal, future providers — without ever importing PSP-specific code. Architecture invariant enforced by grep guards: no OxidEsales\Payments\Stripe or OxidEsales\Payments\PayPal references in opalreturns/src/.

How it plugs in · three integration points
flowchart LR subgraph PSP["PSP modules (peers)"] ST["Stripe
StripeRefundRequestEvent"] PP["PayPal
PayPalRefundRequestEvent"] end subgraph PB["Payment Base · the shared spine"] EV["EventDispatcher
(PSR-14)"] PR["PaymentRefundedEvent"] META["Contract metadata
(setMetadata / getMetadata)"] end subgraph OR["OpalReturns (PSP-agnostic)"] RH["ReturnHandler

The three patterns OpalReturns uses
A
Subscribe to PaymentRefundedEvent
PSP-agnostic. Whether the refund came from Stripe or PayPal, the event is the same shape. OpalReturns’ ReturnHandler hooks the event and triggers the return workflow.
B
Contract metadata for return-specific data
Return reason, RMA number, restocking-fee policy — stored on the Smart-Contract via setMetadata(). Survives the lifecycle, queryable via the contract repository.
C
Resolution broker via tagged services
Tag: opalreturns.resolution_handler. PSP-specific resolution logic lives in each PSP module, not in OpalReturns. Broker is the only fan-out point — same pattern as oe.payment.admin_panel and oe.payment.event_translator.
The lesson: a downstream module never reaches into a PSP. PSP-specific code goes in the PSP module under a tag the downstream module collects. Three real registries in production today: oe.payment.admin_panel, opalreturns.resolution_handler, oe.payment.event_translator.

Principles · what hooks where

A shipment module is a downstream consumer,
just like OpalReturns.

The same pattern that produced OpalReturns produces a shipping integration. Zero PSP imports. Hook the events Payment Base already publishes. Mirror the architecture invariants. Ship faster than any PSP-coupled shipping module ever could.

Architecture invariants enforced
  • No PSP imports. Grep guard in pre-commit blocks any OxidEsales\Payments\Stripe reference.
  • No direct contract mutations. Dispatch events. Handlers mutate.
  • Tagged services for PSP-specific behaviour. Carrier-side code is PSP-independent.
  • Shared admin tab. Contribute a panel via oe.payment.admin_panel or its shipping-side equivalent.

Build a Shipment module · 2 of 4
Event handlers · the shipping logic

Three handlers carry the shipping flow.
All three subscribe to Payment Base events.

1. Reserve stock on contract creation
class StockReservationHandler implements HandlerInterface
{
    public static function getHandledEventClass(): string
    {
        return ContractCreatedEvent::class;
    }

    public function handle(object $event): void
    {
        $contract = $event->getContext()->getContract();
        foreach ($contract->getBasket()->getItems() as $item) {
            $this->inventory->reserve(
                articleId: $item->getArticleId(),
                quantity: $item->getQuantity(),
                contractId: $contract->getId()
            );
        }
    }
}
2. Create shipment on payment capture
class ShippingFulfillmentHandler implements HandlerInterface
{
    public function __construct(
        private readonly CarrierAdapterRegistry $carriers,
        private readonly ShipmentRepository $shipments,
        private readonly LoggerInterface $logger,
    ) {}

    public static function getHandledEventClass(): string
    {
        return PaymentCapturedEvent::class;
    }

    public function handle(object $event): void
    {
        $orderId = $event->getContext()->getOrderId();
        $carrier = $this->carriers->get($this->pickCarrierFor($orderId));

        try {
            $shipment = $carrier->createShipment(
                $this->buildRequestFor($orderId)
            );
            $this->shipments->save($shipment);
        } catch (\Throwable $e) {
            $this->logger->error(
                'Shipment creation failed',
                ['orderId' => $orderId, 'err' => $e->getMessage()]
            );
            // Don't rethrow — other handlers continue.
        }
    }
}
3. Release stock on cancel / expire
class StockRestorationHandler implements HandlerInterface
{
    public static function getHandledEventClass(): string
    {
        // Multi-event handlers register one class per event,
        // or use a registered alias under the same priority.
        return ContractCancelledEvent::class;
    }

    public function handle(object $event): void
    {
        $contractId = $event->getContext()->getContract()->getId();
        $this->inventory->releaseReservation($contractId);
    }
}

// services.yaml · same handler, two events
StockRestorationHandler:
    tags:
      - { name: payment.event_handler, priority: 0 }
StockRestorationHandlerOnExpiry:
    class: StockRestorationHandler
    tags:
      - { name: payment.event_handler, priority: 0 }
    # event class chosen via factory + handles ContractExpiredEvent
Best practices baked in
  • Idempotency. Webhooks may fire twice. Check oe_payments_idempotency via IdempotencyRepositoryInterface before acting.
  • Don’t rethrow. One slow carrier call must not block the rest of the chain.
  • Queue slow work. Hand label creation to a queue; event handlers stay fast.
  • Test the handler in isolation. Mock interfaces, not classes.
Notice what’s absent: no StripeClient. No PayPalApi. The shipping module is genuinely PSP-agnostic. If we add Klarna tomorrow, the shipping module learns nothing about it — the event arrives identically because Payment Base owns the event shape.

Build a Shipment module · 3 of 4
Carrier adapters · data model · admin tab contribution

Carriers are the new PSPs.
One CarrierAdapterInterface, N implementations.

Carrier abstraction · mirrors PaymentAdapter
interface CarrierAdapterInterface
{
    public function quoteRate(QuoteRateRequest $r): RateResponse;
    public function createShipment(ShipmentRequest $r): ShipmentResponse;
    public function cancelShipment(string $trackingNumber): bool;
    public function trackShipment(string $trackingNumber): TrackingStatus;

    public function getCarrierName(): string;
    public function getSupportedCountries(): array;
    public function supportsFeature(string $feature): bool;
}

// 3 concrete impls behind a registry, picked by config + region
class DhlAdapter   implements CarrierAdapterInterface { /* … */ }
class UpsAdapter   implements CarrierAdapterInterface { /* … */ }
class FedExAdapter implements CarrierAdapterInterface { /* … */ }

// Tagged registry — same SOLID pattern as PSPs
CarrierAdapterRegistry:
    arguments:
      - !tagged_iterator shipping.carrier_adapter
DhlAdapter:
    tags: [{ name: shipping.carrier_adapter, region: EU }]
Where data lives
  • Tracking number. On the contract via $contract->setMetadata('tracking_number', …) — queryable on the order detail page without a join.
  • Shipment record. Module’s own table (oe_shipping_shipment) keyed on contract ID. Survives the contract.
  • Carrier choice / rate / SLA. Module’s table (oe_shipping_quote). Linked to BasketSnapshot hash for reproducibility.
  • Audit trail. Reuse oe_payments_transaction for shipping events — or your own table if domain-distinct.
Admin tab · contribute, don’t replace
class ShippingPanelProvider implements PanelProviderInterface
{
    public function __construct(
        private readonly ShipmentRepository $repo,
        private readonly TrackingNumberService $tracking,
    ) {}

    public function supports(Order $order): bool
    {
        return $this->repo->existsByOrderId($order->getId());
    }

    public function render(Order $order): PanelView
    {
        return new PanelView(
            title: 'Shipment',
            template: '@shipping/panel.html.twig',
            data: [
                'shipment' => $this->repo->findByOrder($order),
                'tracking' => $this->tracking->urlFor($order),
            ]
        );
    }
}

# services.yaml
ShippingPanelProvider:
    tags:
      - { name: oe.payment.admin_panel,
          provider: shipping, priority: 50 }
What’s on the panel
  • Carrier name, label PDF download link, tracking number with click-through
  • Last known status from trackShipment() (cached for 5 min)
  • Action buttons: cancel shipment, regenerate label, mark as delivered (admin override)
  • Cost, SLA, weight, dimensions — what the carrier returned at quote time
One tab. Every consumer. Payment Base’s “Payment” tab now hosts: PSP panel(s), OpalReturns panel, Shipping panel. Each is a tagged service. Adding a 5th panel is one YAML entry.

Testing · quality gates · release lifecycle

TDD-first. DevOps-first.
The same gates every Payment Base module ships under.

Test pyramid
  • Unit tests own logic. Mock interfaces, not final classes — if a class is final, extract a seam.
  • Integration tests own the wiring — Doctrine writes, event chains, DI construction.
  • Playwright owns the browser surface. One regression spec per user-facing feature that crosses a frame boundary.
  • Coverage must not shrink between sprints. Enforced in CI.
Sample test · handler in isolation
public function testReservesEachItem(): void {
    $inv = $this->createMock(InventoryService::class);
    $inv->expects($this->exactly(2))
        ->method('reserve');

    $h = new StockReservationHandler($inv);
    $h->handle(new ContractCreatedEvent(
        $contract, new EventContext()
    ));
}
Quality gates · pre-commit
$ ./bin/pre-commit-check.sh

[1/6] PHPCS  (PSR-12) … OK
[2/6] PHPStan (level 6) … OK
[3/6] PHPMD … OK
[4/6] Unit tests … OK
[5/6] Architecture grep guards
      — no PSP imports … OK
      — no direct contract mutations
        in controllers … OK
[6/6] Module activation smoke
      deactivate → activate → clear … OK
SOLID enforced
  • S — one class, one reason to change
  • O — tagged registries over switch ($carrier)
  • L — handlers honour declared input type
  • I — small interfaces; split before 10 public methods
  • D — constructor inject interfaces
Architecture invariants
  • Peers, not dependents. Stripe, PayPal, Shipping module, OpalReturns share Payment Base — never each other.
  • No direct contract mutations. Dispatch, don’t mutate. Grep guard in one-page-checkout/bin/pre-commit-check.sh.
  • One Payment tab. Tagged panel providers contribute — no per-module admin tabs.
  • Shared settings live in Payment Base. Live/test mode, debug flag, capture mode — via PaymentConfigServiceInterface.
  • Drop deprecated immediately. No @deprecated windows on internal code; rename + delete in one commit.
Release shape
  • Composer package; semver; per-module CHANGELOG
  • Doctrine migrations shipped with the module if it owns tables
  • Activation smoke (deactivate → activate → cache-clear) runs in pre-commit when metadata.php changes
  • Reference impls (Stripe, PayPal, OpalReturns) in CI as integration partners
The compounding payoff. Every new module — PSP, returns, shipping, BNPL, marketplace — arrives faster than the one before. The events already exist. The contract lifecycle already exists. The admin tab already exists. The quality gates already exist. Payment Base is the asset; everything else is a tagged service.
